right_of_response.heading: Right of response
right_of_response.body: The City of Des Moines, the Des Moines Police Department, Motorola Solutions, Sourcewell and the Houston-Galveston Area Council were sent detailed questions, with a deadline for comment and factual correction of 5:00 p.m. Central on Friday, September 11, 2026. Responses are pending. Any answer received will be reflected here and in the article; where a custodian does not answer, this exhibit will say so and state what was asked.
right_of_response.note: EDITORIALLY OWNED — patch this block only. Do not summarise, characterise or anticipate a response that has not been received.

standing.grammar_note: Three things are kept apart everywhere in this exhibit: what a document says, which layer of the record it comes from, and which procurement chain or time plane it belongs to.
standing.config_not_use: Configured to share. Not shown to have shared.
standing.config_not_use_long: Every relationship shown from the August 2026 export is a setting in the City's own platform. No transfer, query, hit or viewing record exists in anything produced.
standing.no_dates: The records reviewed do not establish when any sharing relationship was configured.
standing.clerk_file_caveat: The 25-page file is the City Clerk's roll-call file as produced in 2026. Which documents, if any, accompanied Item 32 in the packets distributed to council members is not established by the records obtained.
standing.no_intent: This exhibit reports structure, not motive. Nothing in it establishes concealment, intent or misconduct by anyone, that any description was false, or that anyone was given a wrong impression.
standing.legend_line: Open rings and dashed connectors show settings in the City's own platform export. They do not show that any plate record was sent or viewed.

chapters.heading: “Mistakenly left off”
chapters.body: On September 10, 2021, a vice president at Motorola Solutions signed a two-page form and sent it to a purchasing cooperative in Staples, Minnesota. It is the routine instrument by which a vendor adds items to a cooperative purchasing contract — the kind of contract that lets a city in Iowa buy from a company in Illinois without running its own bid. Field 1 asks what is changing. The answer, in its entirety, was two sentences.
chapters.consequence: Field 3 asks the vendor to “Describe how the product additions fit within the scope of the original RFP.” The answer, complete, is eleven words: “The LPR is a key component of the WatchGuard Mobile Video System.”

chapters.heading: Item 32 of 36
chapters.body: The Des Moines City Council met on the evening of Monday, November 20, 2023. Its third act of the night was to approve the consent agenda — items 3 through 38, thirty-six items, adopted in a single vote, 7–0. The agenda's own footnote calls them “routine items … enacted by one roll call vote without separate discussion unless … Council requests an item be removed to be considered separately.”
chapters.consequence: Item 32 was not removed. It approved $1,500,080 for M500 in-car video systems and Video Manager under a Sourcewell master agreement, and authorised the Mayor to execute a short form agreement and addendum already on file with the City Clerk.

chapters.heading: What the council-facing summary described
chapters.body: The staff document supporting the item, Council Communication 23-519, described the proposition as “purchasing upgraded in-car video systems with installation, implementation, and video evidence management software.” Its synopsis explains why: the existing equipment “has reached the end of supported life,” the replacement has “enhanced 4K camera functions,” and the software integrates body-worn and in-car video into “a single encrypted file which automatically uploads from the field.”
chapters.consequence: All of that is accurate. The M500 is an in-car video system, VideoManager EL is video evidence management software, and the body-worn integration was real. And across the resolution and the council communication — pages 1 to 4 — there is no occurrence of ALPR, LPR, license plate, Vigilant, LEARN, PlateSearch, VehicleManager, hot list, retention or data sharing.

chapters.heading: Twenty-five pages in the clerk's file
chapters.body: The file the resolution points to — produced to RDP in 2026, twenty-five pages, scanned on a city copier — holds the resolution and roll call, the council communication, the two-page Short Form Agreement W24-152, and then four executed vendor addenda. All four bear signatures dated on or within two days of the vote.
chapters.consequence: Twenty-one of those twenty-five pages can be searched in a text layer. Across all of them, plate-reader language appears on one page.

chapters.heading: The sharing clause, where it appears
chapters.body: On page 9 of the 25 pages, in section 4.5 of the Mobile Video Addendum, under the heading “License Plate Recognition Data”: plate-recognition data collected by the City is the City's data, subject to the City's own retention policy — and the City “at its option, may share its LPR data with other similarly situated Law Enforcement Agencies … by selecting this option within Vigilant VehicleManager.”
chapters.consequence: Sharing plate data with another police department required no memorandum of understanding, no council action, no notice and no vendor approval. It required selecting an option. A separate sentence in the same clause restricts logins — not sharing.

chapters.heading: The price list that was not in the file
chapters.body: The document that says what the City was buying, line by line, is Motorola quote 2241626, dated October 23, 2023. It is not in the clerk's file for Item 32; the City produced it to RDP in September 2026. Its arithmetic ties exactly to the number the Council approved: $1,287,000 for 130 in-car systems with five years of cloud video service, $145,500 for installation, removal, deployment and training, and then two plate-reader lines.
chapters.consequence: $67,580 of plate-reader licensing — 4.51 percent of $1,500,080 — priced in a document that was not before the Council. And the licence layer is not the deployment: the packing list shows every one of the 130 units shipping with a component the manufacturer calls an “M500 ALPR DVR.”

chapters.heading: The contract underneath
chapters.body: By the time the Council voted, Des Moines had already bought the plate-reader platform. It did so on a different cooperative contract, from a different company, under a different city agreement, signed by different officials, over the preceding four months. The vendor was Vigilant Solutions, LLC. The cooperative was the Houston-Galveston Area Council. The city instrument was Short Form Agreement W23-383, whose scope reads: “Contractor will provide automated license plate recognition software Products.”
chapters.consequence: The reviewed records show that this earlier plate-reader capability — the hosted platform, three years of commercially acquired national vehicle-location data, and fixed roadside cameras — was acquired administratively, while the November purchase went to the Council. No council action for any of the earlier instruments appears in the records reviewed. Cooperative purchasing is expressly authorised by city code, and the reviewed records do not establish that any of it violated Iowa law or city code. Not a Flock system: the vehicles here are Sourcewell and H-GAC.

chapters.heading: 2023 record → 2026 configuration snapshot
chapters.body: Everything above is dated. Everything below is a snapshot taken on one morning in August 2026.
chapters.consequence: The records reviewed do not establish when each sharing relationship was configured. Nothing below can be connected in time to anything above.

chapters.heading: What the platform is configured to do
chapters.body: On August 19, 2026 the City produced three spreadsheets exported from Vigilant VehicleManager two days earlier. One is a data-sharing report. It lists 155 law-enforcement agencies whose status for receiving Des Moines' plate detections reads “Sharing.” The 2026 platform was configured for sharing relationships across 36 states and the District of Columbia. One hundred forty-one of the 155 are outside Iowa; five rows are typed “Federal.”
chapters.consequence: This is a configuration, not a record of use. 151 of the 155 rows carry no usable date. Because the export is filtered — the filter line is printed in the file — 155 is a floor, not a total. Configured to share. Not shown to have shared.

chapters.heading: The drawer where the use records would be
chapters.body: Every surveillance system raises the same question, and it is not “what can it do.” It is “who checked.” Department policy is reasonable on its face: it limits plate-reader use to enumerated investigative purposes, sets a 30-day retention period, requires that an employee querying the data “enter all information required detailing the reason for the query,” and assigns a supervisor to “perform regular audits of ALPR inquiries.”
chapters.consequence: Answering a records request for those searches, the City said it “has no documents responsive,” that “search logs are not something the City generates or keeps copies of,” that audit material it holds is confidential intelligence data, and that one entry exists from a review of searches — a review of 500 records. Read precisely: the City is not saying the platform keeps no record. And the reviewed executed agreements contain no corresponding City-side audit, inspection or log-access right.

chapters.heading: What these records prove, and what they don't

council_switch.label: What the council-facing summary described (pp. 1–4)
council_switch.explainer: Pressing this dims everything the council-facing summary did not describe. It is a statement about the summary, not about what any council member knew, read, understood or intended. Item 32 was one of thirty-six consent items. Some underlying instruments were incorporated by reference: the resolution authorised execution of “the Short Form Agreement and Addendum on file with the City Clerk.”

hard_cut.line: The records reviewed do not establish when each sharing relationship was configured.

lanes.label: What the City retains
lanes.body: The City stated it has no documents responsive to a request for search logs, and that search logs are not something it generates or keeps copies of. It treats audit material it does hold as confidential intelligence data under Iowa Code §692.8, and says spot audits are complaint-driven.

lanes.label: What the City produced
lanes.body: One internal audit entry, dated 1 October 2025, recording a review of 500 records. Department policy requiring a documented reason for every query and regular audits of ALPR inquiries, issued 8 March 2024 — four months after the purchase.

lanes.label: What the contract allows
lanes.body: Opt-in outbound sharing by setting, with no memorandum, notice, review or approval required. Chained sub-processor consent. Storage location in the vendor's sole discretion. One audit right, running vendor to City.

lanes.label: What any actual transfer is established to show
lanes.body: Nothing. No transfer, query, hit or viewing record appears in anything produced. This is a statement about the record produced, not a statement that no such record exists anywhere.

known.text: A cooperative contract competed for public-safety video surveillance acquired plate readers in September 2021, on a two-page vendor form whose scope answer is one sentence.
Des Moines cited that contract to its Council as evidence the purchase had been competitively bid.
The Council approved $1,500,080 as one of thirty-six consent items, on a description that named in-car video and video evidence management software.
The plate-reader lines — $67,580, or 4.51 percent of the total — were priced in a quote that was not in the clerk's file, and every delivered system carried an “M500 ALPR DVR” component.
The sharing clause was in the file, at page 9 of 25 — the only page of the twenty-one searchable in a text layer where plate-reader language appears.

The reviewed records show the earlier plate-reader capability — platform, national commercial data and fixed cameras — was acquired administratively between July and September 2023, while the November purchase went to the Council.

As of 17 August 2026 the platform was configured for sharing relationships with at least 155 government agencies across 36 states and the District of Columbia, five of them typed Federal, and to receive from 120 of them.
The only audit right in the executed agreements runs from the vendor to the City; the reviewed executed agreements contain no corresponding City-side audit, inspection or log-access right.

unknown.text: That anyone was misled. Consent agendas exist because councils cannot debate thirty-six routine items a night; the staff description of an in-car video purchase was accurate about the in-car video purchase; and the resolution itself pointed to the addendum.
Use. Not one search, alert, hit or transfer appears anywhere in what the City has produced.
Any connection between 2023 and 2026. The sharing relationships cannot be dated, and this exhibit would be false if it implied the November vote produced the configuration.

Which documents, if any, accompanied Item 32 in the packets distributed to council members. The posting copy the Clerk's system generated five days before the vote is two pages — the resolution and nothing else.
How 130 purchased, 126 subscribed, 120 reported operational and 140 Mobile system records reconcile. No document reconciles them.
What “Customer Data” meant in November 2023. The definition chain runs out of the contract to a vendor-hosted addendum that may change from time to time and that prevails in a conflict.
What the “(F)” prefix on 51 rows means, or the “Inactive” prefix on five. Neither is defined in any located documentation.
What fund the account code on the fixed-camera purchase order refers to. No document maps it; it is published as a question only.

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — the correction nobody voted on
sidebars.body: On June 29, 2026 the Council approved a renewal of the plate-reader software under a newer cooperative contract. Under “PREVIOUS COUNCIL ACTION(S)” the staff communication printed: NONE. It also told the Council the software “is used in connection with the body worn cameras, the in-vehicle video systems, and the stationary traffic cameras.” Seven weeks later, answering a records request, the City withdrew that sentence as misstated, saying the traffic cameras “are not connected to any ALPR system.” The City's own platform inventory supports the correction: two fixed plate-reader sites, no traffic cameras. It is a 2026 document and is never spliced into the 2023 chronology.

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — how the systems were counted
sidebars.body: The August 2026 systems export contains 149 top-level system rows — 140 Mobile, 7 IP, 2 Fixed — with 560 camera rows nested beneath them. Counting the seven IP lane units as cameras rather than systems gives the alternative shorthand of 142 systems and 567 cameras. Either convention is defensible. This exhibit uses the first and says so. One Mobile row is literally named “Unit number.”

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — four unit counts
sidebars.body: 130 purchased and licensed. 126 subscribed. 120 reported operational. 140 Mobile system records in the 2026 export. Four numbers, four sources, no reconciling document. This exhibit publishes all four and offers no explanation.

sidebars.heading: Sidebar — a note on Flock
sidebars.body: Des Moines does not run a Flock system; its network is Motorola/Vigilant. One Flock document exists in the City's productions: a data-sharing memorandum of understanding signed for the City by the Chief of Police on February 3, 2026, whose Flock Group, Inc. signature block — signature, name, title and date — is blank, on a memorandum stating it becomes effective “on the last date specified below.”

network_page.title: Explore the configuration
network_page.dek: Every relationship in the City of Des Moines' August 2026 VehicleManager sharing export, as the reader chooses to see it. These are settings, not movements.
network_page.standing_note: Nothing on this page is animated to suggest motion. Counterparties are drawn as open rings, never as filled location dots. No connector is drawn by default. Select a ring to show that one relationship; select a state's label to filter to that state. When you select an agency, one connector appears at once, without direction and without motion, labelled “configured to share.”

records_page.title: The record
records_page.dek: Every instrument, chain, price, date, record layer and receipt behind this exhibit — as a chronology, as two contract chains, as the clerk's document stack, and as a parts list.
records_page.corrections_note: This exhibit is built on a complete-record adjudication dated 3 September 2026 and aligned to article draft v0.2 dated 7 September 2026. Both corrected figures and framings used in earlier RDP working notes. Those corrections are listed here so the older versions are not reintroduced.

corrections.now: 36 states and the District of Columbia
corrections.why: The export's State column holds 37 distinct values, one of which is the District of Columbia.

corrections.now: 149 top-level system rows (140 Mobile, 7 IP, 2 Fixed) with 560 nested cameras
corrections.why: The earlier shorthand counted the seven IP lane units as cameras. Both conventions are defensible; the exhibit states which it uses.

corrections.was: “Council saw the cameras but not the network.”
corrections.now: What the council-facing summary described, versus what the instruments contained, versus what the City had already contracted administratively
corrections.why: Item 32 was one of thirty-six consent items and the resolution incorporated the addendum by reference. Nothing in the record establishes what any member saw, read or knew.

corrections.now: Five change forms identified for contract 010720 in 2021
corrections.why: The 3 September 2021 form created the price list that the 14 September form says the plate reader was left off of.

corrections.was: “Customer Data is defined in the MCA.”
corrections.now: The customer agreement refers onward to a vendor-hosted Data Processing Addendum for that definition
corrections.why: The addendum is at a vendor URL, may be updated from time to time, and states that it prevails in a conflict.

corrections.now: The City stated it has no responsive documents and does not generate or keep copies of search logs
corrections.why: Department policy requires a documented reason for every query and regular audits, and one audit entry reviewing 500 records is in the record. Retention by the City is not the same as existence anywhere.

corrections.now: Two separately dated facts: contractual permission in 2023, observed configuration in 2026
corrections.why: 151 of 155 rows carry no date. No record establishes that chronology.

corrections.was: An arithmetic error in the services subtotal
corrections.why: Recomputed to the cent from the quote's line items; ties exactly to the resolution amount and to the purchase order's five-year schedule.

corrections.was: “The larger surveillance capability did not go through Council at all.”
corrections.now: The reviewed records show the earlier capability was acquired administratively, while the November purchase went to the Council
corrections.why: The narrower proposition is what the ledger supports; the broader one asserts more about council process than the records establish.

corrections.was: “The contracts give the City no right to audit it.”
corrections.now: The reviewed executed agreements contain no corresponding City-side audit, inspection or log-access right
corrections.why: Not found within the instruments reviewed is not the same as nonexistence.
